title_en: Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd. v. National Intellectual Property Administration, PRC, et al. — administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent
ruling_gist_en: In the patent invalidation procedure, the examination of whether a particular amendment to a claim constitutes a 'further limitation' should be based solely on whether the amended claim completely contains all the technical features of the original claim, and whether the amended claim adds technical features compared to the original claim, and whether all the added technical features are recorded in other claims of the original claim set. An amendment in the form of a 'further limitation' to a claim should generally be limited to responding to the grounds for invalidation; where the amendment is ostensibly made to overcome the defects pointed out by the grounds for invalidation but in fact reconstructs the claim, it may be rejected.

full_text_en:
Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd. v. National Intellectual Property Administration, et al. — administrative dispute over invalidation of invention patent

Ruling Summary

In patent invalidation proceedings, the review of whether a claim amendment constitutes a "further limitation" shall be based solely on whether the amended claim completely contains all technical features of the amended claim, and whether the amended claim adds technical features compared to the amended claim, and whether all added technical features are recorded in other claims of the original claim set. A "further limitation" amendment to a claim generally shall be limited to responding to the grounds for invalidation; a de facto reconstruction of the claim under the guise of overcoming the defects identified in the grounds for invalidation may be refused.

Supreme People's Court Administrative Judgment

(2021) Zui Gao Fa Zhi Xing Zhong No. 556

Appellant (Plaintiff at first instance, patentee): Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd. Address: 4th Floor, Building 2, Shangfengyuan, Baijiatuan, Haidian District, Beijing 511.

Legal representative: Li Ziqing, executive director of the company.

Agent ad litem: Fu Jianjun, lawyer at Beijing Long'an Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zheng Xiaojun, lawyer at Beijing Long'an (Zhuzhou) Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at first instance): National Intellectual Property Administration. Address: No. 6, Xitucheng Road, Jimenqiao, Haidian District, Beijing.

Legal representative: Shen Changyu, director general of the Administration.

Agent ad litem: Li Xi, examiner of the Administration.

Agent ad litem: Wan Qi, examiner of the Administration (authorized until November 20, 2021).

Third party at first instance (petitioner for invalidation): Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. Address: Whole Building, Building 6, Zone C, No. 88 Maji Road, China (Shanghai) Pilot Free Trade Zone, Shanghai.

Legal representative: Peter Ronald Denwood, chairman of the company.

Agent ad litem: Luo Rui, lawyer at Beijing Hankun Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Zhang Tao, lawyer at Beijing Hankun Law Firm.

In the case of the appellant Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Zhongke Aosen Company) versus the respondent National Intellectual Property Administration and the third party at first instance Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Apple Computer Shanghai Company) concerning an administrative dispute over the invalidation of an invention patent, the patent in question is owned by Zhongke Aosen Company, with patent number 200480036270.2, titled "A Method for Acquiring a Face Image and Face Recognition Method and System" (hereinafter referred to as the patent-in-suit). In response to Apple Computer Shanghai Company's request for invalidation of the patent-in-suit, the National Intellectual Property Administration issued Decision No. 40531 on the Examination of the Request for Invalidation (hereinafter referred to as the decision under suit), declaring the patent-in-suit completely invalid. Zhongke Aosen Company, dissatisfied, filed a lawsuit with the Beijing Intellectual Property Court (hereinafter referred to as the court of first instance), requesting revocation of the decision under suit and an order for the National Intellectual Property Administration to make a new decision. The court of first instance rendered Administrative Judgment (2018) Jing 73 Xing Chu No. 10897 on December 30, 2020, dismissing Zhongke Aosen Company's claims. Zhongke Aosen Company, dissatisfied, appealed to this Court. After this Court accepted the case on June 7, 2021, it formed a collegiate panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing on September 8, 2021. The appellant's agents ad litem Fu Jianjun and Zheng Xiaojun, the respondent's agents ad litem Li Xi and Wan Qi, and the third party at first instance's agents ad litem Luo Rui and Zhang Tao appeared in court. The case is now concluded.

The basic facts of this case are as follows:

The filing date of the patent-in-suit is May 14, 2004, the priority date is December 12, 2003, and the grant and announcement date is January 9, 2008. The claims as published in the grant of the patent-in-suit are as follows:

Step three: an imaging device captures the face area illuminated by the active light source to obtain a corresponding image;

Step four: the imaging device transmits at least one captured frame of image to an image data processing system, and the image data processing system detects and locates human eyes and/or a human face from the frame of image;

Step five: extracting a human face image from the image and performing feature extraction on the human face image;

Step six: comparing human face features with human face image data in a database;

Step seven: obtaining a recognition result.

2. The method for recognition using a human face image according to claim 1, characterized in that the active light source is an active radiation source, comprising: an infrared light source or a visible light source, or any combination thereof.

3. The method for recognition using a human face image according to claim 1, characterized in that the active light source is a flash.

wherein the total imaging energy generated by the active light source and the ambient light source on the face part is greater than the imaging energy generated by the ambient light source on the face part.

The human face image recognition system according to claim 16, characterized in that the relative positions of the active light source and the imaging device are fixed, and the projection direction of the active light source forms an acute angle with the axis of the camera lens of the imaging device, i.e., between 0 and 90 degrees.

On October 8, 2018, Apple Computer Shanghai Company requested that the National Intellectual Property Administration declare the patent-in-suit completely invalid. The reasons mainly included: insufficient disclosure in the specification, claims not supported by the specification, unclear scope of protection of the claims, lack of novelty of the claims, and lack of inventiveness of the claims.

During the administrative examination procedure for invalidation, Apple Computer Shanghai Company submitted reference documents 1-11. Among them: Reference 1 is U.S. Patent US2001/0031072A1, with a publication date of October 18, 2001, and its Chinese translation. Reference 1 discloses a facial image recognition device and method, and specifically discloses the following technical features (see paragraphs 71-117 of the description corresponding to the first embodiment of Reference 1 and Figure 1): Figure 1 schematically shows the structure of the facial image recognition device according to the first embodiment of the present invention; this facial image recognition device has a camera 101, a first illumination unit 102, a second illumination unit 103, and an image processing unit 104. The first illumination unit 102 and the second illumination unit 103 may be turned on only when a human recognition subject 100 approaches the device; this situation may be realized by sensing whether the human recognition subject 100 approaches the device and turning on the first illumination unit 102 and the second illumination unit 103 (see paragraph 87 of Reference 1). The first illumination unit 102 radiates light from the upper right or upper left of the camera 101 toward the face of the human recognition subject 100 at a certain illuminance. This first illumination unit 102 is an illumination device such as a fluorescent lamp, and radiates light from the upper right or upper left of the camera 101 toward the face of the human recognition subject 100 at a certain illuminance; the second illumination unit 103 radiates light from the lower part of the camera 101 toward the face of the human recognition subject 100 at a certain illuminance (see paragraph 74 of Reference 1). For example, when the illuminance of the first illumination unit 102 is 1A, the illuminance of the second illumination unit 103 is 2A, the total value of 1A and 2A is B (lx), and the illuminance of external light is C (lx), the following relational expression applies: 1A + 2A = B > C. Here, external light is light other than the light from the first illumination unit 102 and the light from the second illumination unit 103, and is light radiated to the human recognition subject 100; for example, in a room, ceiling illumination (fluorescent lamps, incandescent lamps, etc.) at the upper rear of the human recognition subject 100 corresponds to external light; outdoors or near a window, sunlight, etc., may correspond to external light (see paragraphs 84 and 86 of Reference 1). The image processing unit 104 has an image input unit 105, a feature value extraction unit 106, a recognition unit 107, and a registered information storage unit 108. The image input unit 105 inputs a facial image from the camera 101, performs A/D conversion to digitize it, and then sends it to the feature value extraction unit 106 (see paragraphs 90 and 91 of Reference 1). The feature value extraction unit 106 uses the facial image of the human recognition subject 100 obtained from the image input unit 105 to extract feature values, such as intensity information or subspace information; as shown in Figure 6, the feature value extraction unit 106 has a facial region detection unit 106A, a facial part detection unit 106B, and a feature value generation unit 106C; the facial region detection unit 106A detects a facial region from the facial image input at the camera 101; the facial part detection unit 106B detects the positions of eyes and a nose from the detected facial region part (see paragraphs 92, 94, and 95 of Reference 1). The feature value generation unit 106C crops the facial region at a specific size and shape based on the positions of the detected facial parts to generate feature values; here, for example, intensity values of an area of m pixels by n pixels are used as information as they are, and m x n dimensional information is used as a feature vector (see paragraph 96 of Reference 1). The recognition unit 107 performs facial image recognition processing based on the feature values generated by the feature value generation unit 106C; the recognition unit 107 collates identification data stored in the registered information storage unit 108 with the feature values obtained in the feature value extraction unit 106; therefore, the recognition unit 107 identifies who the human recognition subject 100 captured in the camera 101 is, or determines whether he is the corresponding person; when the corresponding person is identified from among the registered persons, the facial image recognition processing may be completed by seeking which registered person's data is most similar. Therefore, to identify the corresponding person from among the registered persons, the person corresponding to identification data having the maximum similarity to the actually captured facial image may be the recognition result (see paragraphs 97, 102, and 104 of Reference 1). In the fourteenth embodiment, an infrared camera 341 is a camera having sensitivity only in the infrared wavelength region. An infrared illumination lamp 342 illuminates the facial part of the human recognition subject 100 with light in the infrared wavelength region. An infrared light blocking body 344 blocks natural light in the infrared wavelength region. Even in the near-infrared wavelength region of 700 nm or greater, sunlight has considerable radiant energy. For fluorescent lamps, however, in the near-infrared wavelength region of 700 nm or greater, the radiant energy is close to about "0". When the infrared camera 341 having sensitivity at 700 nm or greater is used, the influence of external light due to fluorescent lamps used for general lighting may be almost completely eliminated. Regarding the influence of external light caused by sunlight, sunlight in the infrared wavelength region is prevented from radiating to the face of the human recognition subject 100. When the facial image recognition device according to the fourteenth embodiment is installed indoors, to prevent sunlight (natural light) having wavelength components of 700 nm or greater from radiating from outdoors, an infrared light blocking body 344 made of a film or sheet having infrared cut characteristics may be attached to a window 343, or glass having infrared cut characteristics may be attached to the window 343. Through this, regarding sunlight entering through the window 343, only the infrared wavelength component of the sunlight is removed and visible light components pass through, thereby not giving a person an unnatural feeling (see paragraphs 247-257 of Reference 1 and Figures 37-39). Paragraph 259 of Reference 1 recites that the first to fourteenth embodiments may be implemented by variously combining them.

Reference 5 is an international application published under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (i.e., PCT patent application) WO03/034361A1, with an international publication date of April 24, 2003, and its Chinese translation. Reference 5 discloses a system for human facial feature detection and recognition (see paragraph 5 on page 11 of the Chinese translation of Reference 5), which recites: "In another preferred embodiment of the present invention, an eye detection method using infrared (IR) illumination may be utilized to locate eyes on a normal human face, thereby assisting the face detection module 46. In this method, the target is illuminated by a burst of infrared light generated by an IR strobe, the infrared light preferably being coaxial or nearly coaxial with the optical axis of the video camera 21. The IR increases the brightness of the pupils of the human eyes on the video image. By locating this increased brightness region, the face detection module 46 may quickly identify and locate potential faces within the video image. If the IR strobe flashes only within specifically identified video frames, a frame subtraction technique may be used to more easily identify the regions of increased brightness, which correspond to the positions of the human eyes. Accurate identification of the positions of the human eyes has other advantages, namely, such information may also greatly improve the accuracy of facial recognition software."

On June 3, 2019, the China National Intellectual Property Administration (hereinafter "CNIPA") issued the appealed decision, holding that: First, the amended claims 1-3, 5, 6, and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 that refer to claims 1 and 5 (i.e., the relevant claims in the amended text, hereinafter the same) comply with the provisions of Article 69, Paragraph 1 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law") and Section 4.6, Part IV, Chapter 3 of the Patent Examination Guidelines (hereinafter "Patent Examination Guidelines"), but the amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 do not comply with the above provisions. Therefore, the appealed decision took the technical solutions in claims 1-3, 5, 6, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 1 and 5 in the claims set submitted by Zhongke Aosen Company on May 9, 2019, as the basis for examination. Specifically, the specific reasons why CNIPA did not accept the amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 are as follows: Section 4.6.2, Part IV, Chapter 3 of the Patent Examination Guidelines stipulates: "Further limitation of a claim means adding one or more technical features recorded in other claims to the claim to narrow the scope of protection." The amended claim 1 merges the original claims 2, 4, 6, and 7 into the original independent claim 1; the amended claim 4 merges the original claim 3 into the original independent claim 1. That is, in this amendment, different technical features are respectively added to the same claim (original claim 1), simultaneously forming multiple new independent claims (new claims 1 and 4). However, after the original claim 1 is amended in the form of further limitation, it has become a new claim 1 with increased technical features and a narrowed scope of protection, and the original claim 1 no longer exists. Therefore, the amendment of new claim 4 is no longer acceptable. The amended claims 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 have the same defect as above, and are therefore also not acceptable. Second, the technical solutions claimed for protection by claims 1-3, 5, 6, and 8-10 of this patent, compared with the combination of Comparative Document 1, Comparative Document 5, and common general knowledge in the art, do not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Patent Law"); the technical solution claimed for protection by claims 8-10, compared with the combination of the technical solutions between the first, twelfth, and fourteenth embodiments of Comparative Document 1 and the combination of Comparative Document 1 and common general knowledge, also does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law. Among them, compared with the technical solution disclosed in Comparative Document 1, the technical solution claimed for protection by claim 1 has the following distinguishing technical features: (1) (alternative selection of technical feature 1I) the active light source may also be an infrared light source or a combination of an infrared light source and a visible light source; (2) (technical feature 1L) in step four, it further includes the step of detecting and locating the highlight spot caused by the reflection of human eyes in the image, and using the highlight spot to detect and locate the position of the human eyes from the image; (3) (technical feature 1K) after step four, it further includes a step of judging whether the detection of the human eye and/or face is successful; if successful, proceed to step five; otherwise, proceed to step four. Based on the above distinguishing technical features, the technical problem actually solved by the technical solution claimed for protection by claim 1 is: selecting a suitable active light source, improving the accuracy of detection, and providing a processing flow for possible detection failure. CNIPA decided: declare all claims of this patent invalid.

Zhongke Aosen Company disagreed and filed a lawsuit with the court of first instance in September 2019, requesting: revoke the appealed decision and order CNIPA to make a new decision. The facts and reasons were: First, the appealed decision applied the law incorrectly, leading to an error in determining the examination basis. The appealed decision not only held that the parallel independent claims after further limitation were unacceptable but also held that the dependent claims in the original claims set were unacceptable, which does not comply with the provisions of the Patent Law and its Implementing Regulations. Therefore, the appealed decision's determination that the amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 were not acceptable constituted an error in the application of law. Even if the above amendments were not acceptable, the appealed decision's direct declaration of invalidity without examining the dependent claims in the original claims set was also without legal basis. Second, the appealed decision erred in determining the distinguishing technical features of the amended claim 1 compared with Comparative Document 1. Compared with Comparative Document 1, claim 1 should also include technical features 1E and 1F in addition to the distinguishing technical features identified by the appealed decision. The appealed decision's determination that the fourteenth embodiment of Comparative Document 1 disclosed the identified distinguishing technical feature 1 and could be combined with the first embodiment was erroneous. The appealed decision misinterpreted sunlight and illumination light in Comparative Document 1. The fourteenth embodiment of Comparative Document 1 clearly completely blocks ambient light sources and visible light sources through an infrared camera and an infrared light blocking body 344. Therefore, the appealed decision erred in finding the facts, and the amended claim 1 possesses inventiveness. On the premise that claim 1 possesses inventiveness, based on similar reasons, claims 2, 3, 5, 6, and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referring to claims 1 and 5 also possess inventiveness.

CNIPA argued in defense: The appealed decision found the facts clearly, applied the laws and regulations correctly, followed proper procedures, and reached correct conclusions; it requested the dismissal of Zhongke Aosen Company's claims.

Apple Computer Shanghai Company stated: The appealed decision correctly found the facts and reached correct conclusions; it requested the dismissal of Zhongke Aosen Company's claims.

After trial, the court of first instance found the basic facts of this case, including the content of the amended claims of this patent, the relevant content of Comparative Document 1 and Comparative Document 5, and the division of technical features of claims 1, 5, and 8 of this patent.

The court of first instance held: The focus of this case was whether the amendment method of claims 4, 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 submitted by Zhongke Aosen Company on May 9, 2019, could be accepted; and whether the appealed decision's determination that the amended claims of this patent possessed inventiveness under Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law was correct.

First, regarding whether the amendment method of claims 4, 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 of this patent could be accepted.

Article 69 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law stipulates that during the examination of a request for invalidation, the patentee of an invention or utility model patent may amend its claims, but shall not expand the scope of protection of the original patent. Referring to Section 4.6.2, Part IV, Chapter 3 of the Patent Examination Guidelines, further limitation of a claim means adding one or more technical features recorded in other claims to the claim to narrow the scope of protection.

In this case, the amended claim 1 added the technical features of original claims 2, 4, 6, and 7 to the original claim 1. At this point, the original claim 1, after being amended in the form of limitation, was replaced by the newly amended claim 1. The amended claim 4 is a merger of original claim 1 and original claim 3. Since original claim 1 no longer exists due to its replacement by new claim 1, the amended claim 4 should not be accepted. If the simultaneous existence of amended claims 1 and 4 were allowed, it would be equivalent to one independent claim becoming multiple independent claims, thereby expanding the scope of protection of the original claims, which does not comply with the relevant provisions of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law and the Patent Examination Guidelines. Based on the above reasons, the amended claims 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 should also not be accepted. Therefore, the appealed decision's conclusion that the amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 were not acceptable was correct, and the court of first instance affirmed it.

Second, regarding whether the amended claims of this patent possess inventiveness under Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

To determine whether the claimed invention is obvious compared to the prior art, one should usually, based on the closest prior art, analyze the distinguishing features between the claimed invention and the closest prior art, then determine the technical problem actually solved by the invention based on the technical effect that can be achieved by those distinguishing features, and then, starting from the closest prior art and the technical problem actually solved by the invention, determine whether the prior art as a whole provides technical guidance that would motivate a person skilled in the art, when faced with that technical problem, to modify the closest prior art and obtain the claimed invention.

In this case, the appealed decision determined that compared with the technical solution disclosed in Comparative Document 1, the technical solution claimed for protection by claim 1 has the following distinguishing technical features: (1) the active light source may also be an infrared light source or a combination of an infrared light source and a visible light source; (2) in step four, it further includes the step of detecting and locating the highlight spot caused by the reflection of human eyes in the image, and using the highlight spot to detect and locate the position of the human eyes from the image; (3) after step four, it further includes a step of judging whether the detection of the human eye and/or face is successful; if successful, proceed to step five; otherwise, proceed to step four. Based on the above distinguishing technical features, the technical problem actually solved by the technical solution claimed for protection by claim 1 is: selecting a suitable active light source, improving the accuracy of detection, and providing a processing flow for possible detection failure.

Zhongke Aosen Company, on the basis of the above distinguishing technical features, argued that this patent first detects and locates the human eyes through the highlight spot, then locates the face through the human eyes, and finally captures the facial image and performs feature extraction; that is, this patent first locates the local part, then the whole, and finally extracts the features of the whole. In contrast, Comparative Document 1 first detects the whole, then checks the local part, and finally crops the local area to extract features. Therefore, the distinguishing technical features between claim 1 and Comparative Document 1 should also include 1E and 1F.

Combining the technical features 1E, 1L, and 1F in claim 1 of this patent, the technical feature of "detecting and locating the human eye and/or face" in 1E should be understood as "detecting and locating the human eye" or "detecting and locating the human eye and face," and does not explicitly limit the sequence of detecting and locating the human eye and face. Therefore, the relevant technical solution in claim 1 is to first detect and locate the human eye and/or face, then capture the facial image, and perform feature extraction on the facial image. According to the content disclosed in paragraphs 92, 94-96 of the specification of Comparative Document 1, the face region detection unit 106A detects the face region from the facial image input at the camera 101; the face local detection unit 106B detects the positions of the eyes and nose from the detected face region; the feature value generation unit 106C crops the face region at a specific size and shape based on the detected positions of the facial parts to generate feature values. Among them, the operations performed by the face detection region 106A and the face local detection unit 106B disclose the technical feature of "detecting and locating the human eye and/or face" in 1E of this patent; the operations performed by the feature value generation unit 106C disclose the technical feature of "capturing the facial image and performing feature extraction on the facial image" in 1F of this patent. Therefore, the content and sequence of the above steps in Comparative Document 1 are consistent with 1E and 1F in the amended claim 1 of this patent. The technical features 1E and 1F of the amended claim 1 of this patent have been disclosed by Comparative Document 1. Therefore, Zhongke Aosen Company's claim that the appealed decision omitted distinguishing technical features lacks basis. The appealed decision correctly identified the distinguishing technical features between claim 1 and Comparative Document 1.

For distinguishing technical feature 1, according to the content disclosed in paragraphs 253-255 of the specification of Comparative Document 1, the infrared light blocking body 344 is used to block sunlight (natural light) with a wavelength component of 700 nm or more radiated from outdoors, i.e., to block light in the near-infrared wavelength region or larger wavelength region of sunlight (natural light), to prevent these lights from radiating onto the face of the human identification object 100, affecting the imaging quality of the infrared camera, and thereby affecting the recognition performance of the facial image. Therefore, the technical solution of the fourteenth embodiment of Comparative Document 1 does not exclude fluorescent lamps and sunlight (natural light); the infrared light blocking body therein does not completely block ambient light sources and visible light sources. Furthermore, combined with the record in paragraph 259 of Comparative Document 1 that "the first to fourteenth embodiments can be implemented in various combinations," there is no technical obstacle to combining the technical solution of the fourteenth embodiment of Comparative Document 1 with that of the first embodiment. On this basis, using multiple active light sources and ambient light sources in cooperation to capture clearer images in daily life is common general knowledge in the art. Combined with the content disclosed in Comparative Document 1, the technical solution of using an infrared light source alone or a combination of an infrared light source and a visible light source as the active light source is obvious. Therefore, Zhongke Aosen Company's claim that the fourteenth embodiment of Comparative Document 1 did not disclose distinguishing technical feature 1 and is mutually exclusive with the first embodiment lacks basis.

Given that Zhongke Aosen Company did not object to the non-obviousness of distinguishing technical features 2 and 3 in its complaint or at trial, the court of first instance will not comment further. Therefore, claim 1 does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

Claim 2 refers to claim 1, and its additional technical feature is: "the total imaging energy produced by the active light source and the ambient light source on the face is greater than twice the imaging energy produced by the ambient light source on the face." According to the illuminance of the first lighting unit 102, the illuminance of the second lighting unit 103, and the illuminance of external light disclosed in Comparative Document 1, it can be determined that the total imaging energy produced by the active light source and the ambient light source on the face is greater than twice the imaging energy produced by the ambient light source on the face. Therefore, the additional technical feature of claim 2 has been disclosed by Comparative Document 1. Since the claim to which it refers, claim 1, does not possess inventiveness, claim 2 also does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

Claim 3 refers to claim 1, and its additional technical feature is: "in step three, it further includes the step of the imaging device tracking the face for shooting as the active light source illuminates the area." To adapt to face recognition of different people, setting the imaging device and the active light source to be capable of moving up and down and automatically moving left and right is a routine choice for a person skilled in the art. Therefore, since the claim to which it refers, claim 1, does not possess inventiveness, claim 3 also does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

Based on the same reasons as claim 1, claim 5 also does not possess inventiveness.

Claim 6 refers to claim 5, and its additional technical feature is: "the total imaging energy produced by the active light source and the ambient light source on the face is greater than twice the imaging energy produced by the ambient light source on the face." Based on the same reasons as claim 2, since the claim to which it refers does not possess inventiveness, claim 6 also does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

Based on the same reasons as claim 1, claim 8, which refers to claims 1 and 5, also does not possess inventiveness.

Claim 9 refers to claim 8, and its additional technical feature is: "the projection direction of the active light source is parallel to the axis direction of the camera lens of the imaging device." Setting the projection direction of the active light source parallel to the camera axis direction to increase the projection brightness of the active light source and thereby increase the imaging energy formed by the active light source on the face is a routine choice for a person skilled in the art. Therefore, since the claim to which it refers, claim 8, does not possess inventiveness, claim 9 also does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

Claim 10 refers to claims 8 and 9, and its additional technical feature is: "the active light sources are symmetrically arranged around the imaging device." To make the irradiation of the active light source on the face more uniform, symmetrically arranging the active light sources around the imaging device is a routine choice for a person skilled in the art. Therefore, since the claims to which it refers, claims 8 and 9, do not possess inventiveness, claim 10 also does not possess inventiveness as provided in Article 22, Paragraph 3 of the Patent Law.

In summary, the court of first instance held that the appealed decision found the facts clearly, applied the laws and regulations correctly, and followed proper trial procedures. Zhongke Aosen Company's litigation reasons were not sustainable and were not supported. In accordance with Article 69 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the court of first instance entered the following judgment: "The claims of the plaintiff, Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd., are dismissed. The case acceptance fee is RMB 100, to be borne by the plaintiff, Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd."

Zhongke Aosen Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to this Court, requesting: to set aside the first-instance judgment and the decision under review, to order the National Intellectual Property Administration to make a new decision, and to have the National Intellectual Property Administration bear the litigation costs of this case. The main facts and reasons are: (1) The decision under review erred in finding that amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12 and claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 were not accepted for non-compliance with Article 69(1) of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law and Section 4.6 of Chapter 3, Part IV of the Patent Examination Guidelines. 1. From a textual interpretation, the provision in the Patent Examination Guidelines that "further limitation of a claim means adding one or more features recorded in other claims to the claim to narrow the scope of protection" does not prohibit further limiting one independent claim into two or more parallel independent claims. 2. From a practical effect, it is very common for a single independent claim to have multiple dependent claims. According to the standard of the decision under review, when the patentee deletes the original independent claim, he can only select one dependent claim, which in essence violates the principle of "disclosure for protection" under the Patent Law. 3. From the specific circumstances of this case, claims 4 and 7 are claims from the original set of claims, not amended claims. The decision under review lacks a basis for excluding unamended claims from the examination basis. Similarly, claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 should also be accepted. Claims 11 and 12 both comply with the provision of adding technical features recorded in other claims to a claim and narrowing the scope of protection, and do not constitute an amendment beyond the scope. (2) The technical solutions of claims 1-3, 5, 6 and claims 8-10 referencing claims 1 and 5 possess inventiveness. 1. The decision under review erroneously identified the distinguishing technical features between claim 1 and Document 1, omitting distinguishing technical features 1E and 1F concerning the detection process and the region for extracting characteristic values. 2. The decision under review erroneously found that distinguishing technical feature 1 of claim 1 compared with Document 1 was disclosed by the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1. 3. For the reasons above, claims 5, 6, 8-10 also possess inventiveness.

The National Intellectual Property Administration argued: The first-instance judgment found clear facts, correctly applied laws and regulations, and had a lawful trial procedure; the appeal should be dismissed and the original judgment affirmed.

Apple Computer Shanghai Company stated: (1) Amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12 and claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 involve amendments beyond the scope of the claims, and such amendments should not be accepted. (2) Even if the above claim amendments were accepted, the relevant claims clearly lack inventiveness, and the conclusion of the decision under review is not improper; to reduce litigation burden, the decision could be affirmed after correcting its reasoning. (3) The finding in the decision under review that amended independent claims 1, 5, 8 and dependent claims 2, 3, 6, 9, 10 lack inventiveness is not improper. Therefore, it requested the dismissal of the appeal and affirmation of the original judgment.

During the second-instance trial of this case, the parties did not submit new evidence and raised no objection to the first-instance judgment's findings on the authenticity, legality, and relevance of the evidence involved.

This Court finds upon trial: The facts found by the first-instance court and the decision under review are true, and this Court confirms them.

This Court holds: The priority date of this patent (December 12, 2003) falls after the effective date of the Patent Law as amended in 2000 (July 1, 2001) and the Implementing Regulations as amended in 2002 (February 1, 2003), but before the effective date of the Patent Law as amended in 2008 (October 1, 2009) and the Implementing Regulations as amended in 2010 (February 1, 2010). The examination of the conditions for granting this patent shall apply the Patent Law as amended in 2000 and the Implementing Regulations as amended in 2002. The amendment of the claims of this patent (May 9, 2019) occurred after the effective date of the Patent Law as amended in 2008 (October 1, 2009) and the Implementing Regulations as amended in 2010 (February 1, 2010), but before the effective date of the Patent Law as amended in 2020 (June 1, 2021). The examination of the conditions for amending the claims of this patent shall apply the Patent Law as amended in 2008 and the Implementing Regulations as amended in 2010. The issues in dispute in the second-instance trial of this case are: whether amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12 and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 should be accepted, and if so, whether their inventiveness should be further examined in the second-instance proceeding; and whether amended claims 1-3, 5, 6 and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 1 and 5 possess inventiveness.

(I) Regarding whether amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12 and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 should be accepted, and if so, whether the inventiveness of the above claims should be further examined in the second-instance proceeding

In this case, the examination of whether amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12 and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 should be accepted shall be conducted in accordance with the provisions of the Patent Law and its Implementing Regulations, and with due consideration of the specific guidance in the Patent Examination Guidelines.

1. On the dimensions of examining claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings

Allowing a patentee to amend claims in patent confirmation proceedings is conducive to substantively incentivizing and protecting innovation, and can effectively prevent inventions with technical contributions from being left unprotected merely due to improper patent claim drafting. However, since the patent has already been granted and the relevant legal order is stable at this time, it is also necessary to impose restrictions on amendments to avoid serious impairment of the public's reliance interests and continuous fluctuation in the stability of the legal order. Therefore, claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings aim at substantively incentivizing innovation and protecting the patentee's legitimate interests as institutional goals, while maintaining the stability of the legal order, avoiding impairment of public reliance interests, and ensuring the operability and efficiency of administrative examination as institutional costs. Restrictions on claim amendments should follow the basic principle of enabling the achievement of institutional goals, and on this basis, control institutional costs as much as possible. Hence, claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings should neither be too lenient, causing serious impairment of reliance interests or continuous fluctuation of the legal order, nor be too mechanical and strict; if restrictions on amendments are too severe due to concerns over institutional costs, the effectiveness of the system will be greatly diminished, and may even render the institutional goals unattainable, which would be counterproductive.

The legal framework governing the acceptance of claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings primarily consists of Article 33 of the Patent Law and Article 69(1) of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law. At the same time, the Patent Examination Guidelines provide specific operational guidance. Whether an amendment to a claim should be accepted involves at least the following aspects:

First, the requirement regarding the scope of amendment. The maximum scope of amendment to claims in patent confirmation proceedings must not exceed the "information scope" stipulated in Article 33 of the Patent Law and the "scope of protection" stipulated in Article 69(1) of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law. Specifically, Article 33 of the Patent Law provides: "An applicant may amend his patent application documents, but the amendment to the invention or utility model patent application documents shall not go beyond the scope of the original description and claims, and the amendment to the design patent application documents shall not go beyond the scope of the original drawings or photographs." Accordingly, amendments to claims in patent grant proceedings must not exceed the entire information scope of the invention disclosed in the original description and claims. By a fortiori reasoning, amendments to claims in patent confirmation proceedings are naturally also limited by this. Article 69(1) of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law provides: "During the examination of a request for invalidation, the patentee of an invention or utility model patent may amend the patent claims, but shall not expand the scope of protection of the original patent." Accordingly, amendments to claims in patent confirmation proceedings must also not exceed the scope of protection of the original patent. Delineating the statutory limits on the scope of claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings from the two dimensions of "information scope" and "scope of protection" is not only conducive to maintaining the basic systemic logic of the Patent Law of disclosure for protection, but also beneficial to balancing the interests of those with genuine technical contributions in obtaining patent grants and the public's reliance on the granted patent text.

Second, the requirement regarding the method of amendment. The aforementioned "information scope" and "scope of protection" are only the statutory maximum limits for claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings. However, not all amendments within the so-called "information scope" and "scope of protection" should be accepted. Whether an amendment can be accepted also requires consideration of the stability of the legal order, the impairment of public reliance interests, and the operability and efficiency of administrative examination. Therefore, the National Intellectual Property Administration may specify and appropriately limit the methods of claim amendment through the Patent Examination Guidelines. The methods of claim amendment in patent confirmation proceedings currently permitted by the Patent Examination Guidelines are generally limited to deletion of claims, deletion of technical solutions, further limitation of claims, and correction of obvious errors. Among these, further limitation of claims grants the patentee relatively flexible and lenient amendment possibilities compared to deletion of claims, deletion of technical solutions, and correction of obvious errors. The Patent Examination Guidelines define an amendment by further limitation as "adding one or more technical features recorded in other claims to a claim to narrow the scope of protection." Therefore, when determining whether a particular method of amending a claim constitutes a "further limitation," the National Intellectual Property Administration need only examine: (1) whether the amended claim completely contains all the technical features of the claim being amended; (2) whether the amended claim adds new technical features compared to the claim being amended; and (3) whether all the added technical features originate from other original claims. If the amended claim does not completely contain any original claim, or if the new technical features added compared to the claim being amended do not originate from other original claims, then the amendment method may be a "rewriting" or "secondary generalization" of the claim rather than a "further limitation."

Third, the requirement regarding the purpose of the amendment. The patent confirmation proceeding is a procedure that, after a patent claim has been granted, examines the justification of the grant based on invalidation grounds when a request for invalidation is filed by another party. It is neither a comprehensive review of the justification of the grant nor an optimization procedure for claim drafting. Therefore, amendments to claims in patent confirmation proceedings should generally be limited to responding to the invalidation grounds (including those raised by the invalidation requester or supplementary evidence, and invalidation grounds or evidence introduced by the National Intellectual Property Administration that were not mentioned by the invalidation requester). Amendments made under the guise of overcoming defects pointed out by invalidation grounds but in reality serving to optimize claim drafting, i.e., non-responsive amendments, may not be accepted because they do not conform to the institutional positioning of the patent confirmation proceeding. Otherwise, it is not difficult to imagine that if non-responsive amendments were accepted, the patent confirmation proceeding would inevitably be transformed into a tool for obtaining additional opportunities to optimize claim drafting after grant. This is not conducive to improving quality from the outset of drafting and grant, nor to the proper functioning of the invalidation request procedure, and would also lead to an imbalance in the interests of the public, including relevant stakeholders, after patent grant. Therefore, for non-responsive amendments, even if they do not exceed the so-called "information scope" and "scope of protection" and fall within the amendment methods permitted by the Patent Examination Guidelines, they may still not be accepted. For example, if a claim amendment lacks a corresponding invalidation request and grounds, it may generally be rejected directly without further examination of its scope and method. As another example, within the same administrative examination proceeding, if the invalidation grounds directed at a claim have already been responded to through an amendment to that claim and the amended claim has been accepted, further separate amendments to that original claim and the resulting additional new claims may generally be rejected because they no longer have any object to respond to.

It is notable that in patent confirmation proceedings, unamended claims are naturally part of the examination basis and do not constitute the object of evaluation for statutory or other restrictions on claim amendments. Therefore, when confirming the examination basis, it should first be clarified whether the relevant claim is an original claim or a new claim formed through amendment. Whether a claim has been amended should be examined substantively, based on whether the scope of protection of the claim before and after the amendment has substantially changed. Generally speaking, mere changes in claim numbering, simple conversions between dependent and independent claim drafting styles, or simple splitting of claims containing parallel technical solutions that do not substantially affect the scope of protection do not constitute an amendment to the claim.

2. On whether the decision under review's failure to accept amended claims 4, 7, 11, 12 and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 was correct

(1) On whether amended claims 4 and 7 should be accepted

The decision under review found that amended claim 4 resulted from merging original claim 3 into original independent claim 1, and claim 7 resulted from merging original claim 13 into original independent claim 9. Zhongke Aosen Company appealed, arguing that amended claims 4 and 7 were original claims of this patent and, being unamended, could not possibly involve amendments beyond the scope. The National Intellectual Property Administration argued, and Apple Computer Shanghai Company stated, that the finding in the decision under review was not improper.

This Court holds: Amended claims 4 and 7 are respectively original claims 3 and 13. In substance, they are not derived from merging original claims 1 and 3, or original claims 9 and 13, respectively. First, a dependent claim is typically drafted in the form of "reference part + limiting part." In particular, the reference part merely specifies the number of the referenced claim without full citation, for the purpose of refining the wording and clarifying the dependency. When the patentee does not intend to amend the original dependent claim, but the claim (independent claim or other earlier dependent claim) to which that original dependent claim refers no longer exists due to amendment, there is no longer an object for numbering reference, nor a need to clarify the dependency. The expression of the reference part in the original dependent claim must necessarily change from a numerical reference to a full citation. However, the substantive content and scope of protection of that claim do not change due to this change in expression. In other words, the new formal independent claim is the original dependent claim itself, not a claim derived from amending the original dependent claim. Second, the so-called merging of claims involves incorporating all the technical features of multiple claims to be merged into one claim, which is one method of further limiting a claim. The amended claim contains and only contains all the technical features of the merged claims. In principle, the scope of protection of the amended claim should be narrower than, and not equal to or wider than, the scope of protection of any of the merged claims. A dependent claim itself contains and only contains all the technical features of the claim it references and its additional technical features. The so-called new claim derived from merging a dependent claim with the claim it references has substantive content and scope of protection identical to those of the original dependent claim. Such a merger is neither necessary nor effective and does not conform to the basic connotation of claim merging. In this case, the substantive content and scope of protection of amended claim 4 are completely identical to those of original claim 3. The only difference between the two is that amended claim 4 uses a full-text expression for the content corresponding to original claim 1, while original claim 3 expressed it by numerical reference. Therefore, amended claim 4 is original claim 3, not a claim merged from original claims 1 and 3. Similarly, amended claim 7 is original claim 13, not a claim merged from original claims 9 and 13.

In summary, amended claims 4 and 7 are both original claims of this patent, not new claims formed through amendment. They are naturally part of the examination basis, and there is no issue of non-acceptance due to so-called amendment. The decision under review's failure to accept amended claims 4 and 7, thereby excluding them from the examination basis, lacks factual basis. Zhongke Aosen Company's relevant appeal contentions should be sustained.

(2) On whether the technical solutions in amended claims 8-10 referencing amended claims 4 and 7 should be accepted

The decision under review found that amended claims 8-10 reference the non-accepted amended claims 4 and 7, and therefore the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 should not be accepted. Zhongke Aosen Company appealed, arguing that amended claims 4 and 7 are original claims of this patent and should be accepted, and thus the technical solutions in amended claims 8-10 referencing amended claims 4 and 7 should also be accepted. The National Intellectual Property Administration argued, and Apple Computer Shanghai Company stated, that the finding in the decision under review was not improper.

This Court holds: As discussed above, amended claims 4 and 7 are respectively original claims 3 and 13 and are naturally part of the examination basis. The decision under review's finding that the technical solutions in amended claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7 should not be accepted, on the ground that amended claims 4 and 7 should not be accepted, lacks basis. Zhongke Aosen Company's relevant appeal contentions should be sustained.

(3) On whether amended claims 11 and 12 should be accepted

The decision under review's reason for not accepting amended claim 4 was: "After original claim 1 has been amended by further limitation, it has become a new claim 1 with increased technical features and a narrowed scope of protection. At this point, original claim 1 no longer exists, so the amendment to new claim 4 is no longer accepted." Its reason for not accepting amended claims 11 and 12 was the same. From this, it can be inferred that the reason for not accepting claim 11 was: after original claim 15 was amended by further limitation to form amended claim 8, original independent claim 15 no longer existed, and there was no basis for further limiting it again to form amended claim 11; and amended claim 12, as a dependent claim of claim 11, should also not be accepted. According to the aforementioned examination rationale that claim amendments in patent confirmation proceedings should be limited to responding to invalidation grounds, the decision under review's handling of amended claims 11 and 12 was not improper.

3. On whether the second-instance court should further examine the inventiveness of amended claims 4, 7 and the technical solutions in claims 8-10 referencing claims 4 and 7

As stated above, the China National Intellectual Property Administration should have accepted but did not accept the amended claims 4, 7, and 8-10. Therefore, the decision under review did not evaluate the inventiveness of the above claims. Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. argued that even if the above claims should be accepted, they are clearly not inventive, and the court of second instance should examine their inventiveness and uphold the decision under review after correcting the grounds. Both Zhongke Aosen Company and the CNIPA argued that if the amendment of the relevant claims should be accepted, it would not be appropriate to continue the trial, and the CNIPA should conduct a new examination and make a decision.

This Court is of the opinion that, because the CNIPA did not accept the amended claims 4, 7, and the technical solutions of claims 8-10 that refer to claims 4 and 7, the parties did not engage in substantive debate on the issue of inventiveness, and the CNIPA also did not evaluate this. Therefore, it is appropriate for the CNIPA to conduct a new examination and make a decision. According to Article 24, Item 1 of the Provisions (I) of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in the Trial of Administrative Cases Involving Patent Grant and Confirmation, where the decision under review is erroneous in its determination of some of the claims in the claims, but correct as to the others, the people's court may, in accordance with Article 70 of the Administrative Procedure Law, render a judgment of partial revocation. Accordingly, this Court revokes the part of the decision under review that declared amended claims 4, 7, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 of this patent invalid, and orders the CNIPA to make a new examination decision in response to the invalidation request filed by Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. regarding the amended claims 4, 7, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 of this patent.

(2) Whether the amended claims 1-3, 5, 6, and the technical solutions of claims 8-10 referring to claims 1 and 5 are inventive

The decision under review found that: compared with the technical solution disclosed in Document 1, the technical solution claimed in claim 1 has three distinguishing technical features, among which distinguishing technical feature 1 is: "the active light source may also be an infrared light source or a combination of an infrared light source and a visible light source." Claim 5 also has this distinguishing technical feature compared with Document 1. Regarding this distinguishing feature, the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 discloses that the facial image recognition device may have an infrared illumination lamp 342 (see paragraphs 247-257 of the specification corresponding to the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1). On this basis, it is common general knowledge in the art to use a variety of active light sources and ambient light sources to capture clearer images in daily life. A person skilled in the art, based on the disclosure of Document 1, could obviously obtain the technical solution of using an infrared light source alone or a combination of an infrared light source and a visible light source as the active light source. Although the technical solution of the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 involves an infrared light blocking body 344, it only blocks natural light in the infrared wavelength region. As can be seen from paragraphs 250-255 of its specification, it does not exclude the presence of illumination light (such as fluorescent lamps) or natural light (such as sunlight). Moreover, Document 1 also clearly provides the technical teaching that "the first to fourteenth embodiments can be implemented in various combinations" (see paragraph 259 of Document 1). Therefore, there is no technical obstacle to combining the technical features related to the "infrared light source" in the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 with the technical solution of the first embodiment.

Zhongke Aosen Company appealed, arguing that: 1. The amended claim 1 is inventive. First, the decision under review omitted the distinguishing technical features 1E and 1F between claim 1 and Document 1 regarding the detection process and the feature extraction region. Claim 1 of this patent first locates the local part, then locates the whole; Document 1 first detects the whole, then detects the local part. Second, the decision under review erroneously found that distinguishing technical feature 1 was disclosed by the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1. The fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 explicitly uses an infrared camera and an infrared light blocking body 344 to completely block the ambient light source and visible light, and it does not disclose distinguishing technical feature 1. 2. The amended claims 5 and 8 are inventive. Claims 5 and 8 also have the distinguishing technical feature that the active light source may be an infrared light source or a combination of an infrared light source and a visible light source compared with Document 1, which is not disclosed by the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1. 3. Based on the inventiveness of the amended claims 1, 5, and 8, their dependent claims, namely the amended claims 2, 3, 6, 9, and 10, are also inventive.

The CNIPA argued in its defense, and Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. stated in its submissions, that the determination of the decision under review that the amended independent claims 1, 5, and 8 and the dependent claims 2, 3, 6, 9, and 10 are not inventive is correct.

This Court is of the opinion that Zhongke Aosen Company's assertion that the decision under review erroneously found that distinguishing technical feature 1 was disclosed by the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 lacks a basis, and its appeal claim that the amended claims 1-3, 5, 6, and the technical solutions of claims 8-10 referring to claims 1 and 5 are all inventive cannot be sustained. The specific analysis is as follows:

1. Whether the decision under review omitted distinguishing technical features

The amended claim 1 of this patent makes the following limitations: first, "Step 4: the imaging device transmits at least one captured frame to the image data processing system, and the image data processing system detects and locates human eyes and/or a human face from the frame image"; second, "Step 5: intercepting a face image from the image, and performing feature extraction on the face image"; third, "in Step 4, it also includes a step of detecting and locating high-brightness spots caused by the reflection of light from the eyes in the image, and using the high-brightness spots to detect and locate the position of the eyes from the image." From the content of the above claims, Step 4 can detect and locate human eyes, human faces, or both from the captured image, and it does not limit the order of detection and location of the face and eyes; Step 5 and the limitation regarding the high-brightness spots of eye reflection in Step 4 also cannot be interpreted to imply a detection order. Zhongke Aosen Company's assertion that the decision under review omitted distinguishing technical features lacks a basis, and this Court does not support it.

2. Whether distinguishing technical feature 1 is disclosed by the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1

First, the role of the infrared camera in the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 is to sense the infrared active light source; a high-sensitivity infrared camera with a sensitivity of 700 nm or more can also exclude the influence of fluorescent lights. In this regard, paragraph 249 of Document 1 states: "the infrared camera 341 is a camera that is sensitive only in the infrared wavelength region." Paragraph 254 explicitly states: "when using the infrared camera 341 having a sensitivity of 700 nm or more, the influence of external light due to fluorescent lamps used for general lighting can be almost completely eliminated." The reason is that, according to Figures 38 and 39 and paragraph 253 of Document 1, "in the near-infrared wavelength region of 700 nm or greater, the radiant energy (of fluorescent lamps) is approximately '0'." In other words, the reason why a high-sensitivity infrared camera above 700 nm can exclude the influence of fluorescent lights is not because limiting the use of an infrared camera is equivalent to limiting the absence of fluorescent light sources, but because the radiation range of the fluorescent light source and the sensitivity range of the high-sensitivity infrared camera happen to be offset. Therefore, even if there are fluorescent lights in the usage environment, the high-sensitivity infrared camera will not be disturbed.

Second, the role of the infrared light blocking body in the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 is to block natural light in the infrared wavelength region; it cannot block natural light of other wavelengths. Paragraph 255 of Document 1 explicitly states this: after natural light passes through the infrared light blocking body, "only the solar light component of the infrared wavelength is removed and the visible light component is transmitted, thereby not giving a sense of incongruity."

In summary, based on the limitations of the infrared camera and the infrared light blocking body in the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1, it is difficult to conclude that this embodiment cannot be used in combination with fluorescent lamps or natural light. Therefore, given that paragraph 259 of Document 1 explicitly states that "the first to fourteenth embodiments can be implemented in various combinations," the determination of the decision under review that there is no technical obstacle to combining the technical features related to the "infrared light source" in the fourteenth embodiment of Document 1 with the technical solution of the first embodiment is correct.

In conclusion, the appeal request of Zhongke Aosen Company is partially established. The facts found in the first-instance judgment are basically clear, but the application of law is partially erroneous, and it should be revoked. In accordance with Article 70, Item 2, and Article 89, Paragraph 1, Item 2 of the Administrative Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the judgment is as follows:

(1) Revoke the Administrative Judgment (2018) Jing 73 Xing Chu No. 10897 of the Beijing Intellectual Property Court;

(2) Revoke the part of Decision No. 40531 on Invalidation Request Review of the China National Intellectual Property Administration that declared the amended claims 4, 7, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 of the invention patent No. 200480036270.2, titled "A Method for Acquiring Face Images and a Face Recognition Method and System," invalid;

(3) The China National Intellectual Property Administration shall make a new examination decision in response to the invalidation request filed by Apple Computer Trading (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. regarding the amended claims 4, 7, and claims 8-10 referring to claims 4 and 7 of the invention patent No. 200480036270.2, titled "A Method for Acquiring Face Images and a Face Recognition Method and System";

(4) Dismiss the other claims of Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd.

The first-instance case acceptance fee is RMB 100, and the second-instance case acceptance fee is RMB 100, to be borne by Beijing Zhongke Aosen Technology Co., Ltd. and the China National Intellectual Property Administration, respectively, in the amount of RMB 50 each.

This judgment is final.
